The mentioned splitting schemes give a second-order error in the computed
averages, but surprisingly each gives an exact result for computed averages of either
position or momentum. The exactness property is not born out of the symmetry of
the method, but rather of the speciﬁc order of terms and choice of splitting “building
blocks”. Even non-symmetric ﬁrst-order schemes can exhibit similar qualities. For
example, analysis shows that the schemes denoted AOAB or BAOA both exhibit
a ﬁrst order error in the covariance hqpih D O.h/, however they give exact results
for both hq2ih and hp2ih.
7.4.2
More General Schemes
We can conduct a similar analysis for any integrator that we can express in the
form (7.7), simply by plugging in the relevant constants and solving a linear
equation. The difﬁculty lies when random numbers are reused, leading to correlation
between steps. This requires careful treatment to compute the expectation.

number between steps:

schemes, we are able to compute the exact expected average by solving the linear
equations. The results are summarized in Table 7.1, where we have not considered
the AOBOA and BOAOB schemes due to their inconsistency at large friction
(this does not preclude the analysis, but limits each those method’s usefulness in
simulation). Similar analysis can be conducted for more complicated composition
schemes involving multiple force evaluations.
The mentioned splitting schemes give a second-order error in the computed
averages, but surprisingly each gives an exact result for computed averages of either
position or momentum. The exactness property is not born out of the symmetry of
the method, but rather of the speciﬁc order of terms and choice of splitting “building
blocks”. Even non-symmetric ﬁrst-order schemes can exhibit similar qualities. For
example, analysis shows that the schemes denoted AOAB or BAOA both exhibit
a ﬁrst order error in the covariance hqpih D O.h/, however they give exact results
for both hq2ih and hp2ih.
7.4.2
More General Schemes
We can conduct a similar analysis for any integrator that we can express in the
form (7.7), simply by plugging in the relevant constants and solving a linear
equation. The difﬁculty lies when random numbers are reused, leading to correlation
between steps. This requires careful treatment to compute the expectation.

number between steps:

The behavior of the methods can thus be summarized as
\[|\langle q^2\rangle_h^{[ABOBA]}-\langle q^2\rangle|=O(\epsilon h^2),\qquad
|\langle q^2\rangle_h^{[BAOAB]}-\langle q^2\rangle|=O\left(\frac{\epsilon^2h^2}{1+\gamma^2}+\epsilon^2h^4\right),\]
\[|\langle q^2\rangle_h^{[OBABO]}-\langle q^2\rangle|=O(h^2),\qquad
|\langle q^2\rangle_h^{[OABAO]}-\langle q^2\rangle|=O(h^2).\tag{7.15}\]
The twofold surprising result though, is that (a) the leading error of the $[BAOAB]$ scheme has behavior proportional to $\epsilon^2$, while (b) the leading order term of the $[BAOAB]$ scheme is annihilated for large $\gamma$.

The flows of each of these systems individually preserves the Gibbs distribution: denoting the Fokker-Planck operators associated to these flows by $\mathcal L_H^\dagger$ and $\mathcal L_O^\dagger$ we have
\[\mathcal L_H^\dagger\rho_\beta=0,\qquad\mathcal L_O^\dagger\rho_\beta=0,\]
and hence
\[\exp(t\mathcal L_H^\dagger)\rho_\beta=\exp(t\mathcal L_O^\dagger)\rho_\beta=\rho_\beta.\]
We can consider the propagation of measure resulting from a numerical discretization defined by the composition of these two pieces. For a scheme $[HO]$, we have the distribution first propagated under Hamiltonian dynamics, and then the momenta are evolved as the solution to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, which clearly will preserve the Gibbs measure
\[\exp(h\mathcal L_O^\dagger)[\exp(h\mathcal L_H^\dagger)\rho_\beta]=\exp(h\mathcal L_O^\dagger)\rho_\beta=\rho_\beta.\]

corrected_json.statement_latex:
Given any divergence free vector field $f$, we have
\[-\nabla\cdot(f\rho)=-f\cdot\nabla\rho,\]
thus $\mathcal L_f^\dagger\rho=-\mathcal L_f\rho$.
If $\mathcal L_f$ preserves a first integral $I$, then $\mathcal L_f$ preserves any distribution which is a function of $I$. It follows that any energy-preserving, divergence free vector field will always preserve the Gibbs distribution.

As an example of such a $J$-splitting, we may take $K=N_c$ with each $J_i$ to be defined by the components of the canonical symplectic structure matrix having to do with the $i$th position and momentum pair, thus the equations of motion for the $i$th vector field become
\[\dot q_i=p_i/m_i,\qquad \dot p_i=-\frac{\partial U}{\partial q_i}(\bar q_1,\ldots,\bar q_{i-1},q_i,\bar q_{i+1},\ldots,\bar q_{N_c}),\]
where components with a bar over them are fixed during the calculation. This is, itself, a Hamiltonian system with a single degree of freedom $q_i$ and the potential $\widehat U_i(q_i)$ obtained by freezing all other components in the original potential function. Any such 1-dof Hamiltonian system is formally integrable (albeit in quadratures).

For example, for the method labelled by the string $[ABAO]$, we have
\[\exp(h\widehat{\mathcal L}_{[ABAO]})=\exp((h/2)\mathcal L_A)\exp(h\mathcal L_B)\exp((h/2)\mathcal L_A)\exp(h\mathcal L_O),\]
where importantly note the apparent reversal of the sequence of products, known as the vertauschungssatz (see the discussion in [164, Section III.5.1]), which is a consequence of the relation
\[\phi(\mathcal U_t^{f_1}(z))=(e^{t\mathcal L_{f_1}}\phi)(z),\]
for some vector field $f_1$ with associated flow map $\mathcal U_t^{f_1}$ and generator $\mathcal L_{f_1}$, where the choice of $\phi(z)=\mathcal U_t^{f_2}(z)=(e^{t\mathcal L_{f_2}}\mathrm{Id})(z)$ demonstrates this reversal. We will find it more convenient to work with the adjoint of the perturbed generator, denoted $\widehat{\mathcal L}^\dagger$, which we may compute as
\[\exp(h\widehat{\mathcal L}_{[ABAO]}^\dagger)=\exp(h\mathcal L_O^\dagger)\exp((h/2)\mathcal L_A^\dagger)\exp(h\mathcal L_B^\dagger)\exp((h/2)\mathcal L_A^\dagger).\]

for some finite truncation index $n\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. The remainder term at order $h^{n+1}$ will involve the integration of finitely many derivatives of its argument. Hence for observables of sufficient smoothness with compact support, this remainder term will remain bounded (see [223]).

We can make use of Taylor’s theorem to write the identity
\[P_h=P_0+h\left.\frac{dP_t}{dt}\right|_{t=0}+\cdots+\frac{h^n}{n!}\left.\frac{d^nP_t}{dt^n}\right|_{t=0}
+\frac{h^{n+1}}{n!}\int_0^1(1-\lambda)^n\left.\frac{d^{n+1}P_t}{dt^{n+1}}\right|_{t=\lambda h}d\lambda,\]
for some finite truncation index $n\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$. The remainder term at order $h^{n+1}$ will involve the integration of finitely many derivatives of its argument. Hence for observables of sufficient smoothness with compact support, this remainder term will remain bounded (see [223]).

audit.explanation: 按已披露的范围，三个Printed/别名定义忠实记录原文的“点谱、几何单重”部分，corrected是较弱的点谱候选而不是已经证明的结论。原文“离散谱即单重谱”是实质数学疑误；此外几何单重不能代替代数单重，完整的原书谱论含义仍需人工选定，因此整体NEEDS_HUMAN，不将源文错误隐改后判PASS。
audit.counterexample: 在E=ℂ³上取L=diag(0,−1,−1)、ρ=e₁。有限维算子具有紧预解式，零特征空间恰为span{ρ}，非零特征值在左半平面，但−1的特征空间是二维，故紧预解式不推出simpleEigenvalue。另取二维零特征值Jordan块可见几何重数1也不保证代数重数1。
audit.suggested_fix: 人工确认原书勘误和simple的含义。完整修正版应明确函数空间、闭算子及其定义域、紧预解式资格、孤立谱与有限代数重数，并以独立条件处理零特征值唯一性和左半平面位置；现有较弱Prop可保留，但不能命名成已验证谱定理。

audit.explanation: correctionSolvable是任意实模线性自映射L下rhs属于range(L)的命题，数学含义正确。但没有ρβf1结构、零质量归一条件、Fredholm相容性、紧预解式/定义域、指数稳定或全局半群存在。JSON明确只登记目标，不证明预期；原书也明确未给严格结果，必须保留并NEEDS_HUMAN，不能把紧预解式及有界扰动升级为无条件可解性。

By composing the semigroup operators
\[\exp(h\mathcal L_{[XYZ]}^\dagger)=\exp(h\mathcal L_Z^\dagger)\exp(h\mathcal L_Y^\dagger)\exp(h\mathcal L_X^\dagger),\]
and computing the terms in the BCH expansion, we have
\[\widehat{\mathcal L}_{[XYZ]}^\dagger=\mathcal L_{LD}^\dagger+h\mathcal L_{1,[XYZ]}^\dagger+O(h^2),\]
where
\[\mathcal L_{1,[XYZ]}^\dagger=-\frac12([\mathcal L_X^\dagger,\mathcal L_Y^\dagger]+[\mathcal L_X^\dagger,\mathcal L_Z^\dagger]+[\mathcal L_Y^\dagger,\mathcal L_Z^\dagger]).\tag{7.20}\]
The first order correction function for this scheme is then given by the particular solution to the PDE,
\[\mathcal L_{LD}^\dagger(f_{1,[XYZ]}\rho_\beta)=-\mathcal L_{1,[XYZ]}^\dagger\rho_\beta.\tag{7.21}\]

First, note that if we define the function $g(q,p)$ as
\[g(q,p)=\beta p^TM^{-1}\nabla U(q),\]
then through simple computation we have
\[\mathcal L_A^\dagger\rho_\beta=-\mathcal L_B^\dagger\rho_\beta=g(q,p)\rho_\beta.\]
This is particularly useful as
\[[\mathcal L_A^\dagger,\mathcal L_B^\dagger]\rho_\beta=(\mathcal L_A^\dagger\mathcal L_B^\dagger-\mathcal L_B^\dagger\mathcal L_A^\dagger)\rho_\beta=-(\mathcal L_A^\dagger+\mathcal L_B^\dagger)(g(q,p)\rho_\beta)=(\mathcal L_O^\dagger-\mathcal L_{LD}^\dagger)(g(q,p)\rho_\beta).\]
Now notice that for a function $\psi(q)$ purely of position, we have
\[\mathcal L_{LD}^\dagger(\psi(q)\rho_\beta)=-(p^TM^{-1}\nabla\psi(q))\rho_\beta(q,p),\]
and hence we can compute
\[\mathcal L_O^\dagger(g(q,p)\rho_\beta)=\gamma\rho_\beta(-p\cdot\nabla_pg(q,p)+\beta^{-1}\nabla_p\cdot M\nabla_pg(q,p))=-\gamma g(q,p)\rho_\beta=\gamma\beta\mathcal L_{LD}^\dagger(U(q)\rho_\beta).\]

If we define the function $g(q,p)$ as $g(q,p)=\beta p^TM^{-1}\nabla U(q)$, then through simple computation we have
\[\mathcal L_A^\dagger\rho_\beta=-\mathcal L_B^\dagger\rho_\beta=g(q,p)\rho_\beta.\]
\[[\mathcal L_A^\dagger,\mathcal L_B^\dagger]\rho_\beta=-(\mathcal L_A^\dagger+\mathcal L_B^\dagger)(g\rho_\beta)=(\mathcal L_O^\dagger-\mathcal L_{LD}^\dagger)(g\rho_\beta).\]
For a function $\psi(q)$ purely of position, we have
\[\mathcal L_{LD}^\dagger(\psi(q)\rho_\beta)=-(p^TM^{-1}\nabla\psi(q))\rho_\beta(q,p),\]
and hence we can compute
\[\mathcal L_O^\dagger(g(q,p)\rho_\beta)=\gamma\rho_\beta(-p\cdot\nabla_pg+\beta^{-1}\nabla_p\cdot M\nabla_pg)
=-\gamma g\rho_\beta=\gamma\beta\mathcal L_{LD}^\dagger(U(q)\rho_\beta).\]

Let $M=\beta=1$ and define the biased double-well potential as
\[U(q)=(q^2-1)^2+q/2.\]
We shall consider computing the average of a specific observable $\vartheta(q,p)$, and estimating the error due to discretization using the correction functions given in (7.25), where we choose the observable
\[\vartheta(q,p)=p^2-qU'(q)+2qp,\qquad\langle\vartheta\rangle=0.\]
The first order correction term for the $[BOA]$ scheme is given by the formula
\[\langle\vartheta f_{1,[BOA]}\rangle=\frac\beta2\int_{\mathcal D}(p^2-qU'(q)+2qp)(pU'(q)+\gamma U(q)-c)\rho_\beta d\omega
=\frac1\beta+\frac\gamma2\langle U\rangle-\frac{\gamma\beta}{2}\langle qUU'\rangle=\frac{2-\gamma}{2\beta}.\]
Hence for the critical value of $\gamma=2$, the leading order correction will be zero, giving
\[\langle\vartheta\rangle_h^{[BOA]}=\langle\vartheta\rangle+O(h^2).\]

corrected_json.label: Lemma 7.1
corrected_json.statement_latex:
Lemma 7.1 Consider two numerical schemes with associated operators governing the evolution of measure $ST$ and $TS$, with unique associated invariant distributions $\widehat\rho_{ST}$ and $\widehat\rho_{TS}$ respectively, such that
\[ST\widehat\rho_{ST}=\widehat\rho_{ST},\qquad TS\widehat\rho_{TS}=\widehat\rho_{TS}.\]
Under suitable ergodicity assumptions (such that in the long-time limit, all distributions converge to the invariant distribution), we have
\[\widehat\rho_{ST}=S\widehat\rho_{TS},\qquad\widehat\rho_{TS}=T\widehat\rho_{ST}.\]
corrected_json.proof_latex:
If we assume that $\lim_{n\to\infty}(ST)^n\rho=\widehat\rho_{ST}$, for any initial distribution $\rho$, then we have
$\widehat\rho_{ST}=\lim_{n\to\infty}(ST)^n\widehat\rho_{ST}=\lim_{n\to\infty}S(TS)^{n-1}T\widehat\rho_{ST}=S\widehat\rho_{TS}$.
A similar statement holds for $\widehat\rho_{ST}$.
corrected_json.proof_note: 原页推导与上下文全文见original_page_text；数学符号的排版以随附原页PDF为准。

As we are in the overdamped regime, we would expect that this scheme should
have an O.h4/ D O.2/ error in conﬁgurational averages, while inheriting the
other properties of the BAOAB scheme for the harmonic and perturbed harmonic
models considered in Sects. 7.4 and 7.5. Moreover, since we completely remove the
second order term in the Langevin dynamics conﬁgurational density expansion, we
expect to observe this behavior across all values of h and . This is quite a surprising
result, given the qualitative similarity between Eqs. (7.39) and (7.40).
The beneﬁt of (7.40) over the Euler-Maruyama scheme is that we can get second
order accuracy in averages with only a single evaluation of the force at each
timestep. However, our analysis presented here is only for the inﬁnite time case.
For averages computed in ﬁnite time, work in [224] has shown that (7.40) does
indeed give a ﬁrst order error, albeit one that vanishes exponentially fast in time as
the simulation progresses. Hence for suitably long simulations, the observed error
will be O.h2/.
We can think of the noise process in (7.40) as corresponding to a colored noise
which has characteristics that directly depend on the stepsize, although the noise
decorrelates in just a couple of timesteps. This is therefore no longer a Markov
process, however it can be reformulated as such if one considers the appropriate
extended space (or keeping the momenta pn).
7.11
Applying the Schemes to a Biomolecule
Numerical analysis of a scheme should always be supported (and informed by)
thorough numerical testing. Often salient features of a discretization method can be
missed because of a shallow scope of experimentation. Our goal will be to evaluate

As we are in the overdamped regime, we would expect that this scheme should
have an O.h4/ D O.2/ error in conﬁgurational averages, while inheriting the
other properties of the BAOAB scheme for the harmonic and perturbed harmonic
models considered in Sects. 7.4 and 7.5. Moreover, since we completely remove the
second order term in the Langevin dynamics conﬁgurational density expansion, we
expect to observe this behavior across all values of h and . This is quite a surprising
result, given the qualitative similarity between Eqs. (7.39) and (7.40).
The beneﬁt of (7.40) over the Euler-Maruyama scheme is that we can get second
order accuracy in averages with only a single evaluation of the force at each
timestep. However, our analysis presented here is only for the inﬁnite time case.
For averages computed in ﬁnite time, work in [224] has shown that (7.40) does
indeed give a ﬁrst order error, albeit one that vanishes exponentially fast in time as
the simulation progresses. Hence for suitably long simulations, the observed error
will be O.h2/.
We can think of the noise process in (7.40) as corresponding to a colored noise
which has characteristics that directly depend on the stepsize, although the noise
decorrelates in just a couple of timesteps. This is therefore no longer a Markov
process, however it can be reformulated as such if one considers the appropriate
extended space (or keeping the momenta pn).
7.11
Applying the Schemes to a Biomolecule
Numerical analysis of a scheme should always be supported (and informed by)
thorough numerical testing. Often salient features of a discretization method can be
missed because of a shallow scope of experimentation. Our goal will be to evaluate
the efﬁcacy of the numerical schemes for Langevin dynamics presented thus far. We
shall look at the invariant (long-time) averages resulting from computations using
the four symmetric Langevin integrators that we derived using our splitting, for
which results for the harmonic oscillator are detailed in (7.15), and for which a more
general error analysis was considered in Sect. 7.9.2. Additionally we will compare
their results to the performance of the standard SPV and BBK schemes considered
in Sect. 7.3.2.

(7.40)
As we are in the overdamped regime, we would expect that this scheme should
have an O.h4/ D O.2/ error in conﬁgurational averages, while inheriting the
other properties of the BAOAB scheme for the harmonic and perturbed harmonic
models considered in Sects. 7.4 and 7.5. Moreover, since we completely remove the
second order term in the Langevin dynamics conﬁgurational density expansion, we
expect to observe this behavior across all values of h and . This is quite a surprising
result, given the qualitative similarity between Eqs. (7.39) and (7.40).
The beneﬁt of (7.40) over the Euler-Maruyama scheme is that we can get second
order accuracy in averages with only a single evaluation of the force at each
timestep. However, our analysis presented here is only for the inﬁnite time case.
For averages computed in ﬁnite time, work in [224] has shown that (7.40) does
indeed give a ﬁrst order error, albeit one that vanishes exponentially fast in time as
the simulation progresses. Hence for suitably long simulations, the observed error
will be O.h2/.
We can think of the noise process in (7.40) as corresponding to a colored noise
which has characteristics that directly depend on the stepsize, although the noise
decorrelates in just a couple of timesteps. This is therefore no longer a Markov
process, however it can be reformulated as such if one considers the appropriate
extended space (or keeping the momenta pn).
7.11
Applying the Schemes to a Biomolecule
Numerical analysis of a scheme should always be supported (and informed by)
thorough numerical testing. Often salient features of a discretization method can be
missed because of a shallow scope of experimentation. Our goal will be to evaluate
the efﬁcacy of the numerical schemes for Langevin dynamics presented thus far. We
shall look at the invariant (long-time) averages resulting from computations using
the four symmetric Langevin integrators that we derived using our splitting, for
which results for the harmonic oscillator are detailed in (7.15), and for which a more
general error analysis was considered in Sect. 7.9.2. Additionally we will compare
their results to the performance of the standard SPV and BBK schemes considered
in Sect. 7.3.2.

Indeed, calculating the temperature of the system from an average of kinetic energy by
\[N_dk_BT=\langle p^TM^{-1}p\rangle,\tag{7.41}\]
gives a similar problem. Using Proposition 6.1 we may formulate many alternative functions whose averages are proportional to the system temperature [193, 211, 319]. Such observables are normally based on the periodic forces of the system in order to work in periodic boundary conditions; in the following experiments we shall use the configurational temperature
\[N_dk_BT=\langle q\cdot\nabla U(q)\rangle.\tag{7.42}\]
Were one able to solve the dynamics exactly, the kinetic and configurational temperatures would of course be equal.

[ERRATUM?] 原页两个块复用λ；各子步应有各自的乘子，不能把同一乘子作逐项相加而双计。O子步需随机约束冲量来抵消法向Wiener噪声；有限变差λdt的字面解释通常不成立。Lean用reactionImpulse的修正方向合理，应明标与原印写法的解释差别。
H和O没有对初值及样本的联合可测性资格。OIntegralStep仅对每个固定初值x要求过程可测/几乎处处性质；最后一段O却接收前两段产生的随机初值。没有联合可测性/可测随机核，不能由这些类型推出复合输出是随机变量、满足相应条件分布或把固定初值的零测例外传递到随机初值。

C_signature.fields_and_noise: H=(M⁻¹p,−∇U−g′ᵀλ_H)，O漂移=(0,−γp−g′ᵀλ_O)，constraintReaction的求和方向确为Jacobian转置。ONoise(j)的i分量为δ_ij√(2γθm_i)，位置噪声为零；θ=k_BT时系数与原页相符。
C_signature.H_integral_step: 正质量、g C²、U C¹、T≥0；X连续、X(0)=x0，所有t∈[0,T]都在cotangentConstraint；每个坐标速度/力可积，q和p分别满足相应的0到t积分方程。Λ是时间函数，未当作常乘子。
C_signature.O_integral_step: vectorWiener含P概率、非负时间上的Gaussian/零均值/min协方差/连续样本路径及坐标过程独立；另有正质量、正γ/θ、g C²、T≥0。对每个t分别P-a.e.保持约束、q固定、p满足OU积分方程；P-a.e.路径连续和初值，reaction(0)=0。所有sample的漂移坐标可积；reaction处于g′(x0.q)ᵀ的像，可含随机部分。
C_signature.adaptedness: MeasurableSpace.comap的映射是sample↦(s↦W_s(sample))，s∈[0,t]；不是仅W_t。因而固定初值的X_t和reaction_t对W历史可测，这部分正确；时间索引的几乎处处量词并未直接写成一个全时刻共同事件。

counterexample.type_level_witness: 令l=1、g(q)恒为1，则cotangentConstraint为空。两个MapQualification的∀x∈cotangentConstraint均真，甚至可令P=0、W=0并任取H/O；QualifiedComposition仍接受hH/hO，但P.prod P=0并非概率、W也非Wiener。故最后类型并不无条件规定其注释所称的乘积概率空间。即使限定非空约束及合规输入，也仍须补联合可测性来处理随机初值。
counterexample.random_initial_state_gap: 对每个确定x有P(N_x)=0并不单独给出{(ω,x):ω∈N_x}的乘积可测性。现有O资格允许零测例外依赖x，且没有(sample,x)联合可测性；因此对独立的随机x使用Fubini/条件分布缺少必要前提。这是规格缺口，不声称每个具体O-H-O算法都会失败。
counterexample.printed_multiplier: n=l=1，g(q)=q，m=γ=θ=1，x0=(0,0)。cotangentConstraint迫使q_t=p_t=0；O积分方程要求reactionImpulse_t=√2 W_t，它不是普通有限变差的∫λ_s ds。Lean允许随机冲量合理，原印λdt若按普通有限变差读取则不成立。

higher order solution (see Sect. 3.3.3). Relative to the force calculation, solving the
geodesic drift step (even to high accuracy) can, in typical molecular systems, be
considered computationally cheap. Given these splitting pieces, one may write down
constrained equivalents of any of the schemes described in Sect. 7.3.1.

Multiplying by $e^{\gamma h/2}$ gives
\[|\cosh(\eta h/2)+(h/\eta)\sinh(-\eta h/2)|\le\cosh(\gamma h/2).\]

C_signature.matrix_definitions: Mat2=Matrix(Fin 2)(Fin 2)ℝ；fastMatrix=[[0,1],[-Ω²,-γ]]；slowMatrix(h)=[[1,0],[-h,1]]；fastExponential=exp(h•fastMatrix)；multipleX=slowMatrix(h)·fastExponential(h)，乘法顺序与原页一致。Ω只是实频率参数，并非样本空间类型Ω。
C_signature.characteristicUnitDisk: 对所有z∈ℂ，z²−tr(X)z+det(X)=0→‖z‖≤1；实2×2矩阵的全部复特征根均被覆盖，等价于谱半径≤1，不等价于一般幂有界或随机方差有界。
C_signature.spectralRadiusStability: 对任意实Mat2，在0<d=det X<1前提下，闭单位圆根条件↔|tr X|≤1+d。复共轭根时模为√d<1；实根时p(1)=1−tr+d≥0、p(−1)=1+tr+d≥0结合0<d<1排除越过±1。边界可有简单±1及另一根±d，类型正确。
C_signature.hyperbolicStability: η∈ℂ并取复范数；第二项使用sinh(−ηh/2)，所以等于cosh(ηh/2)−(h/η)sinh(ηh/2)，符号正确；右侧为实cosh(γh/2)。η改成−η不改变左侧。
C_signature.multipleX_bridge: 设F=fastMatrix，B=F+(γ/2)I，则B²=(η²/4)I。η≠0时exp(hF)=e^(−γh/2)[cosh(ηh/2)I+(2/η)sinh(ηh/2)B]，于是det X=e^(−γh)，tr X=2e^(−γh/2)[cosh(ηh/2)−(h/η)sinh(ηh/2)]。γ,h>0给0<det X<1，且1+e^(−γh)=2e^(−γh/2)cosh(γh/2)，故声明的等价式正确。以上是签名的纸面代数核对，不宣称已检查Lean证明。
